1.point: Sufi chains and the Shia list of intercessors both run back through Ali to the Prophet, so the difference between them lies further along the chain; the chapter will show one road, one source, and authority belonging to the Imam.
steps: A familiar Shia list of names (Du'a Tawassul) runs from the Prophet through Ali down to the Imam of the time.
A Sufi order's licence is also a list of names running back to the Prophet, with Ali first after him.
Since the two lists meet at Ali, the difference must lie further along; state what the chapter will establish.

2.point: A Sufi order is a path that, long after the first seekers, hardened into an institution made of a chain, a method and total obedience.
steps: Define tariqa and name the three things that make a path an order: chain, method, demands on the disciple.
Show the orders came late, centuries after the early seekers walked without them.
Show what the institution added: self-devised methods and a system of rites and obedience.
Explain what total obedience asks (the ghusl image) and flag that the last section will ask who may hold it.
Show the chain is a human, contested institution (used again in Section 5).

3.point: Nearly every order's chain ends in Imam Ali, so Sufi and Shia seekers share one source.
steps: State that almost all chains culminate in Ali, citing Tabataba'i's count of orders.
Test the hard case: an order whose head claimed Abu Bakr descent still traces its robe to Ali.
Name the one exception (Naqshbandiyya) to justify the 'almost'.
Note that the chain idea itself, inherited inner knowledge, is a Shia idea the orders keep without the Imams.

4.point: Shia share the orders' path, but because souls differ no one method fits all, so the traveller needs a guide who has walked the road rather than an order's technique.
steps: Shia travellers share the orders' remembrance (and books).
What distinguishes orders is technique; the Suhrawardiyya and Naqshbandiyya run opposite ways.
Both work, so there is no single method and Shia irfan prescribes none.
The reason: each soul is its own channel; grace takes the container's shape.
Many channels does not mean many religions; the ways are many within Islam.
Therefore the traveller needs someone who has walked the road to read his own case (Hasanzadeh and Tabataba'i).

5.point: Shia masters followed shaykhs and gave them real standing, but the authority the orders vest in a chain belongs, for Shia, to the Imams.
steps: Obedience is where Shia part from the orders; the Imamate leaves no room for a chain of authority.
Historically the Shia masters came to stand outside the orders while keeping full loyalty to the law.
Yet they used the orders' forms: robe, shaykh, pledge; three scholars show how far.
What the traveller attains comes from God, not from those forms (Sayyid Haydar).
Through whom it comes: the Imam accompanies the traveller at every rank and this company is the most important condition.
The general teacher can be left, the special teachers never; so a shaykh stands under the Imam, and the Tawassul names are those special teachers.

¶5.label: advance

¶7.label: advance

¶8.label: advance

¶9.label: support

¶10.label: restate

¶11.label: advance

¶12.label: support

¶13.label: support

¶14.label: advance

¶15.label: restate

¶16.label: advance

¶18.label: advance

¶19.label: advance

¶20.label: advance

¶21.label: advance
